name: An AI Literacy Program for the Whole Community
title: An AI Literacy Program for the Whole Community
answer: An AI literacy program for the whole community means that students, teachers and parents all gain some understanding of AI rather than leaving it to a single group. Students learn how AI works, where it helps and fails, and how to use it responsibly at their own level, while staff receive required training and parents are shown what their children learn and how the school uses AI. It matters because an informed community makes parents partners in the work instead of skeptics or bystanders.

sections.body: This idea is a school-wide approach to AI literacy that reaches everyone in the community, not just students. Students need age-appropriate understanding of how AI works, where it helps, where it fails, and how to use it responsibly. Teachers need training in the rules and practices of this Volume, including privacy and the name removal habit, the human review rule, AI use levels, and how to check AI output, along with the pedagogical knowledge described earlier in the chapter. Parents need to see what their children are learning and how the school uses AI. The problem it solves is a community where only some people understand AI, which leaves parents uninformed and staff unprepared for the rules they are expected to follow.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the program runs on three tracks. For students, Chapter 8 sets out a grade band approach, and Chapter 5 describes the ask then check routine for the youngest learners, so what students learn is matched to their age. For staff, training in the rules and practices of this Volume should be required for anyone who uses AI with students or student data, covering privacy and the name removal habit, the human review rule, AI use levels, and how to check AI output, plus the pedagogical knowledge described earlier in the chapter. For parents, parent AI nights described in Chapter 14 are one way to show them what their children are learning and how the school uses AI, and the five questions in Figure 14.5 give parents a way to ask about the school's practices.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites a systematic review of AI literacy in K through 12 (Casal-Otero et al., 2023), which describes a growing body of work on what students should learn at each stage. That is the only evidence the text gives for this idea, and it speaks to student learning rather than to the staff training or parent engagement parts of the program. The text does not offer a study or figure for the required staff training or for parent AI nights, so those elements rest on the practice and reasoning set out in the book rather than on research findings stated here.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on who needs training and what it covers. Training should be required for staff who use AI with students or student data, which means the obligation follows the use of AI and student data rather than being optional. The content of that training is bounded by the rules and practices of this Volume, including privacy and the name removal habit, the human review rule, AI use levels, and how to check AI output. Parents are to be shown what their children are learning and how the school uses AI, and the five questions in Figure 14.5 give them a way to ask about the school's practices. The decisions about what students learn at each stage, what staff must be trained in, and how the school uses AI remain with the people in the school, and the text frames an informed parent as a partner rather than a skeptic or a bystander.
